title: Project Kinetica — From Impact Iteration to Final Technical Art Breakdown
summary: A brief retrospective on separating collision controls, refining material response, and presenting the frozen study through the Showcase and Breakdown.

body.heading: Separate the controls
paragraphs: Project Kinetica connects weapon motion, impact evaluation, localized vertex deformation and material-specific particles. One recorded iteration separated contact area from collision radius: broad weapons could otherwise register contact too early. Keeping those controls separate allowed collision thickness to change without changing the pressure model.

body.heading: Refine the visible response
paragraphs: Slime’s topology and normals were revised to address faceting and uneven highlights. Carapace became Metal so the target and its spark effect expressed the same material idea. These iterations made geometry, naming and visible feedback part of the same authored response.

body.heading: Present the study with its limits
paragraphs: The final presentation brings together a Showcase, Technical Breakdown and public selected source tied to the frozen implementation. The comparison frames show authored responses rather than controlled physical measurements. Vertex displacement does not change topology or collision geometry, and no performance benchmark is claimed.

The retrospective ends at that frozen study. Its useful lesson is to explain both the visible result and the controls behind it; implementation detail and supporting evidence remain in the case study and Breakdown.

title: Project Confluence — From Technical Experiments to District Blockout
summary: The first development phase of Project Confluence connects climate-adaptive urban design with practical UE5 experiments in parameter-driven construction, environmental materials, rendering, and district blockout.

hero.alt: Early Unreal Engine 5 coastal district graybox with terraced terrain, white building masses and a provisional local rail corridor beside the ocean.
hero.caption: Project Confluence · Early coastal district blockout in Unreal Engine 5. Terrain, buildings, and transit geometry remain provisional.

body.heading: Establish an environment direction
paragraphs: Project Confluence is an ongoing Environment Technical Art study exploring climate-adaptive high-density urbanism. Its central idea is that a future city continuously adapts its inherited infrastructure instead of replacing it.

The worldbuilding direction combines mountainous island settlements, dense mixed-use development, ecological infrastructure, and rail-based public transportation. Local trams follow the islands' urban corridors, while cross-sea railways belong to a separate regional network.

The current production focus is one representative coastal district, not the entire city. Establishing a coherent relationship between everyday urban life, steep terrain, public transit, and the ocean is the first environment design challenge.

The District Master Plan v0.1 explores how the station, neighborhood streets, residential areas, public spaces, and vertical circulation might connect across three terrain levels. These are planning proposals that still require validation in Unreal Engine.

media.alt: District Master Plan v0.1 showing proposed station, neighborhood and residential zones at 30m, 50m and 70m, with walking routes, public spaces and vertical connections.
media.caption: District Master Plan v0.1 · Proposed spatial organization and circulation. Planning diagram; not completed geometry.

body.heading: Explore parameter-driven construction
paragraphs: Before beginning the formal environment, I used a separate UE5 sandbox to learn Blueprint workflows through small experiments.

One procedural Actor uses exposed module count, mesh, and spacing parameters to construct repeated Static Mesh Components in the editor. The Construction Script allows changes to regenerate the arrangement without manually replacing each component.

The two examples demonstrate the same Blueprint with different module counts and spacing values. This establishes a basic parameter-driven construction workflow without committing to a full procedural city system.

media.alt: Unreal Engine editor showing five repeated mesh modules; Module Count is 5 and Spacing is 150.
media.caption: Five modules generated with a spacing parameter of 150.

media.alt: Unreal Engine editor showing three repeated mesh modules; Module Count is 3 and Spacing is 250.
media.caption: Three modules generated with a spacing parameter of 250.

media.alt: Blueprint graph looping from zero to module count minus one, adding Static Mesh Components, setting their mesh and placing them along Z using index multiplied by spacing.
media.caption: Blueprint construction logic · Iterating over module count, adding Static Mesh Components and assigning relative positions.

body.heading: Prototype environmental wetness
paragraphs: The next experiment focused on material behavior. After exploring Material Instances, Material Functions, UVs, and world-aligned mapping, I developed an initial MF_WaterlineWetness prototype.

The function calculates a height-based wetness mask using world-space position relative to an adjustable waterline. Additional noise controls introduce variation along the boundary and transition region.
The tests separate the visible material response from the underlying mask, making it easier to inspect where the transition occurs.

media.alt: Concrete test column with a subtle height-based wetness material transition on its lower surface.
media.caption: Initial waterline wetness material test on a concrete surface.

media.alt: Test column with a contrasting diagnostic mask revealing the waterline transition and an irregular boundary.
media.caption: Diagnostic visualization of the height-based wetness transition and boundary variation.

body.heading: Investigate real-time rendering
paragraphs: Further experiments explored exposure, atmospheric fog, Lumen global illumination, reflections, and Nanite visualization.

A simple red-surface lighting study was used to inspect how material color and indirect illumination influence surrounding surfaces. The experiments helped establish an initial understanding of Unreal Engine's rendering workflow before environmental art production.

media.alt: Red test column standing on a light floor in a simple Unreal Engine lighting study.
media.caption: UE5 lighting study · Red surface and surrounding floor used to inspect indirect illumination and color contribution.

body.heading: Begin the coastal district blockout
paragraphs: With the initial engine studies completed, I created the formal ProjectConfluence project and its first working level, L_District_Blockout_01.

The current Landscape covers approximately 252 × 504 meters, with three principal terrain elevations around 30m, 50m, and 70m. Initial graybox work establishes building masses, a local coastal tram corridor and station, bridge approaches, steep terrain, and distant-island context.
The first blockout prioritizes terrain hierarchy, transit alignment, building placement, and the overall relationship between the inhabited terraces and the ocean.

The current planning iteration examines how the station area, middle neighborhood street, upper residential zone, and connecting pedestrian routes might form a coherent district. These circulation proposals have not yet been fully implemented.

media.alt: Top-down district graybox showing terraced coastal terrain, preliminary white building masses and a long local rail corridor.
media.caption: District graybox · Top-down view of the three-tier coastal layout, preliminary building masses, and local rail corridor.

body.heading: Scope and next steps
paragraphs: Confluence remains in early development.
The current district is a graybox environment, while the Blueprint, material, and rendering experiments were developed separately in the UE5 learning sandbox.
Procedural city generation, dynamic water behavior, final environmental assets, and the full transit system have not yet been implemented.
The next phase focuses on validating pedestrian circulation, architectural massing, terrain connections, and transit geometry before developing more advanced procedural environment tools.
The objective is to build a coherent, technically grounded environment rather than expand the city before its fundamental spatial relationships are resolved.
